newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese police say HK immigration rumours calmed.
newsitem.headline: Chinese police say HK immigration rumours calmed.

text.p: Senior Chinese police claimed victory on Wednesday in heading off a rush of illegal immigrants to Hong Kong by making arrests and scotching rumours of an amnesty when the British colony reverts to Beijing rule in July.

Speaking at a rare news conference, officials of the Ministry of Public Security stressed that China's re-establishment of sovereignty over Hong Kong after 156 years of colonial rule would not unleash the gates to a flood of Chinese migrants.

Beijing, coordinating with Hong Kong authorities, had set in place strict rules and quotas on entry of mainland Chinese to Hong Kong -- and these were unchangeable, Xu Ganglu, director general of the Bureau of Exit and Entry Control, said.
He said his announcement last week that no amnesty would be granted to women and children who entered Hong Kong illegally had calmed a flood of attempts to sneak into the territory.
"These amnesty stories have been exploited by unscrupulous elements who have taken the opportunity to charge exorbitant sums to mainland residents and smuggling them into Hong Kong," he said.
"People should not believe such gossip," he said.
Several of those involved had been arrested, Xu said. He did not give details.
Hundreds of Hong Kong parents pay human smugglers, known as snakeheads, to spirit their China-born children into the British colony.

Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, warned on Monday the rules would not be relaxed after the handover and that children smuggled in would be deported. He plans to visit the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou on Sunday to discuss the problem.
Hong Kong operated a quota system, allowing 150 people from mainland China, including 45 mainland-born children, into the territory each day to join their families, Xu said.
All illegal immigrants would be sent back from Hong Kong, he said. "There are no exceptions."
In an unusual display of force on Tuesday, Hong Kong immigration officers seized an eight-year-old girl and her mother from their family home and deported them to China.
Senior Hong Kong immigration official Leung Ping-kwan said the deportations sent a signal that there would be no amnesty for illegal immigrants.
The Chinese side was equally adamant.

"As Hong Kong's population density is very high and its resources are limited, we will stick to the method of approving a limited quota of visitors," Xu told reporters, adding that China would hold firm despite an increase in applications from mainland Chinese eager to see Hong Kong before the July 1 handover.
"We are confident that we can uphold the entry and exit procedures for Hong Kong," Xu said. "We have no doubt at all."
Under current quotas, 810 mainland Chinese are allowed into Hong Kong every day to visit relatives and 900 are permitted to go in as tourists, Xu said.
As for mainland Chinese children of people holding permanent residency of Hong Kong, about 40,000 of 90,000 whose applications had been recognised as valid had already entered Hong Kong, he said.
Some 30,000 had received formal approval from Hong Kong immigration authorities and were in a queue to enter Hong Kong, with the remainder awaiting the relevant paperwork, he said.

Most of them were fathered by Hong Kong men and born to mainland Chinese women. Both the mother and the children have to apply for residency rights to join their husbands in Hong Kong -- a process which can take years.
